rewrite.text: I'd like to talk about swimming, which I only learned at nineteen. Growing up in Dhaka, I never had the chance, partly because there was no pool nearby and partly because my parents were wary of the river. In my first year at university, a friend mentioned a women-only session at the sports complex, so I decided to give it a go. The coach, a retired national swimmer, was endlessly patient. For the first fortnight I couldn't even put my face in the water, but she broke everything down into manageable steps: breathing, then floating, then kicking with a board. Three months later I swam my first full length without stopping. It keeps me fit, but more importantly, it showed me that I can master something difficult as an adult as long as I'm patient with myself. These days I swim every Saturday morning, and last summer I even taught my younger cousin.

These days, a growing number of young people take a year out between finishing school and starting university, usually to work or to travel. Although this break can delay a student's education, I believe the benefits are greater than the drawbacks.

The main advantage of a gap year is that it gives young people experience of real life. Working in a shop or a restaurant teaches responsibility, time management and how to deal with different kind of people. Travelling abroad, on the other hand, broadens their horizons and makes them more independent, because they have to solve problems without their parents' help. As a result, many students return with a clearer idea of what they want to study, so they are less likely to change course or drop out later.

However, there are some disadvantages that should be considered. Firstly, a year without studying may cause students to lose their academic habits, and some of them find it difficult to return to classes. Secondly, travelling is expensive, so only students from wealthy families can afford a gap year abroad, which seem unfair. There is also a risk that a student who starts a well-paid job decides never to go to university at all.

In my view, these problems can be avoided with careful planning. Students can set a clear goal for the year, such as saving money for tuition or doing volunteer work related to their future degree, and universities can offer a deferred place so that the student know they have somewhere to return to.

In conclusion, while a gap year has some risks, I am convinced that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages, as long as it is used purposefully.

Nowadays many young people take a gap year after school. They work or travel before they go to university. In my opinion this has more advantages than disadvantages.

First, a gap year give students experience of life. If they work in a shop they learn responsibility and how to talk with different kind of people. If they travel to other countries they become more independent because their parents are not there. Also they can think about what they really want to study, so they will not change their subject later. For example, my cousin worked in a café for one year and now she is more confident. It is also good for their CV.

On the other hand there are some disadvantages. Students can forget how to study and it is difficult for them to go back to the classes. Also travelling is very expensive and not every family have enough money for it. This is not fair for poor students. Some students find a job and earn money and then they never go to university, this is a big problem for their future.

But I think these problems can be solved. Students should make a plan for the year, for example save money for university or do a volunteer work. Universities can also keep a place for the student so they can come back after one year.

In conclusion, a gap year has some problems but I think the advantages are more than the disadvantages if the students use the year in a good way.

Lecturer: Today, seed dispersal by ants, or myrmecochory. Many plants attach a fatty structure called an elaiosome to their seeds. Ants carry the seed to their nest, eat the fat and discard the seed on a waste heap. This protects it from seed-eating beetles, and the soil around the nest is rich in nutrients. Ants typically move seeds no more than ten metres.
In Australia the practice is most common in heathland. Researchers marked seeds with paint to follow them. A problem is that some invasive ants eat the seeds instead of burying them, so conservationists now place seeds close to the nests of native ants.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Beavers were hunted out of Britain by the sixteenth century, prized for their fur and for castoreum, a secretion once used in medicine and perfume. For four hundred years the rivers of England and Scotland flowed without the dams and wetlands these animals build.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 2009 a small trial began in Knapdale, Scotland, where four families of beavers from Norway were released into a chain of lochs. Scientists monitored them for five years. A separate and unplanned population was found on the River Tay in 2012, probably descended from escaped captive animals, and the government decided to let it stay.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The benefits became clear quickly. Dams slow the flow of water, which reduces flooding downstream, and the ponds behind them trap sediment that would otherwise cloud the river. In a trial in Devon, a wetland created by two adults held back much of the water during storms that threatened a nearby village, although some villagers remained unconvinced.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes the animals. Farmers on low-lying land report that burrows weaken riverbanks and that felled trees block drainage ditches. Anglers once feared that dams would stop salmon from migrating upstream, but studies suggest that fish pass over the structures during high water; the evidence for trout is less certain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Wildlife managers now favour a licensing approach: where a dam causes serious damage it can be modified with a pipe that lowers the pond level, and only as a last resort are animals moved. Supporters argue that the cost of these measures is small compared with the expense of building artificial flood defences.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most schools start lessons at around eight in the morning, a time chosen long before anyone studied adolescent sleep. During puberty the body clock shifts: teenagers tend to fall asleep later and wake later, so a pupil who rises at six-thirty may be functioning on the equivalent of a middle-of-the-night alarm.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 2014 a group of schools in Seattle moved their start time from 7.50 to 8.45. Researchers found that pupils slept an average of 34 minutes longer each night, and that attendance improved. Grades rose by about four per cent in biology, the subject taught first thing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics point to practical problems. Later finishes collide with sports practice and part-time jobs, and bus companies that serve several schools in sequence must redraw their routes at considerable cost. Some parents also worry that children will simply stay up later, cancelling any gain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A few schools have tried compromises. One in Ohio keeps the early start but replaces the first lesson with a supervised study period in which pupils can doze, eat breakfast or catch up on homework. Staff report calmer mornings, though the school has not published figures on results.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The debate is therefore less about whether sleep matters than about who should bear the cost of change. Education authorities that have made the switch tend to describe it as an investment, but the full benefits may take years to measure, and few budgets are set with such patience.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For decades, city planners treated noise as a nuisance to be measured in decibels and reduced. In the 1990s, however, the acoustician Helen Varga proposed that a city has a "soundscape" in the same way that it has a skyline, and that its quality cannot be captured by a single loudness figure. A fountain and a motorway may register the same level, yet people describe the first as restful and the second as stressful.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Varga's team asked residents of four European cities to record the sounds they valued most. Church bells, street musicians and children in playgrounds ranked highly; the hum of ventilation systems did not. Importantly, people who could identify the source of a sound tolerated it better than those who could not, which suggests that familiarity matters as much as volume.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Such findings have begun to influence design. In Lyon, tram operators fitted rubber pads to rails in residential districts, while a Copenhagen housing scheme was arranged around a courtyard so that bedroom windows face away from the road. Designers also use sound deliberately: a water feature can mask traffic more pleasantly than a wall of the same cost.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all attempts have succeeded. A plan to play recorded birdsong in a Berlin shopping street was withdrawn after complaints that it sounded artificial, and shopkeepers said it made their customers uneasy. Planners concluded that sounds imposed from above are judged more harshly than those that arise from everyday activity.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Measurement is also being transformed. Low-cost sensors mounted on lamp posts now record not only loudness but the type of noise, using software trained to tell a siren from a drill. Critics worry about privacy, although the devices capture only sound patterns and not speech, and the data are discarded after analysis.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Varga herself remains cautious. She notes that a quiet street is not always a pleasant one, and that the loneliest districts are often the most silent. The aim, she says, is not a quieter city but one whose sounds tell residents that other people are nearby.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Beavers were hunted out of Britain by the sixteenth century, prized for their fur and for castoreum, a secretion once used in medicine and perfume. For four hundred years the rivers of England and Scotland flowed without the dams and wetlands these animals build.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 2009 a small trial began in Knapdale, Scotland, where four families of beavers from Norway were released into a chain of lochs. Scientists monitored them for five years. A separate and unplanned population was found on the River Tay in 2012, probably descended from escaped captive animals, and the government decided to let it stay.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The benefits became clear quickly. Dams slow the flow of water, which reduces flooding downstream, and the ponds behind them trap sediment that would otherwise cloud the river. In a trial in Devon, a wetland created by two adults held back much of the water during storms that threatened a nearby village, although some villagers remained unconvinced.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes the animals. Farmers on low-lying land report that burrows weaken riverbanks and that felled trees block drainage ditches. Anglers once feared that dams would stop salmon from migrating upstream, but studies suggest that fish pass over the structures during high water; the evidence for trout is less certain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Wildlife managers now favour a licensing approach: where a dam causes serious damage it can be modified with a pipe that lowers the pond level, and only as a last resort are animals moved. Supporters argue that the cost of these measures is small compared with the expense of building artificial flood defences.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most schools start lessons at around eight in the morning, a time chosen long before anyone studied adolescent sleep. During puberty the body clock shifts: teenagers tend to fall asleep later and wake later, so a pupil who rises at six-thirty may be functioning on the equivalent of a middle-of-the-night alarm.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 2014 a group of schools in Seattle moved their start time from 7.50 to 8.45. Researchers found that pupils slept an average of 34 minutes longer each night, and that attendance improved. Grades rose by about four per cent in biology, the subject taught first thing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Critics point to practical problems. Later finishes collide with sports practice and part-time jobs, and bus companies that serve several schools in sequence must redraw their routes at considerable cost. Some parents also worry that children will simply stay up later, cancelling any gain.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A few schools have tried compromises. One in Ohio keeps the early start but replaces the first lesson with a supervised study period in which pupils can doze, eat breakfast or catch up on homework. Staff report calmer mornings, though the school has not published figures on results.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The debate is therefore less about whether sleep matters than about who should bear the cost of change. Education authorities that have made the switch tend to describe it as an investment, but the full benefits may take years to measure, and few budgets are set with such patience.
